disease_info: Schizophrenia is a chronic psychotic disorder characterized by a combination of positive symptoms (such as hallucinations and delusions), disorganized thinking and behavior, and negative symptoms (such as diminished emotional expression, reduced motivation, and social withdrawal) that lead to marked functional impairment. Onset typically occurs in late adolescence or early adulthood, but late-onset cases can occur, especially in women and in the context of medical comorbidities or psychosocial stressors. The course is often chronic with episodic exacerbations, and negative symptoms and cognitive deficits tend to be most strongly associated with long-term disability. It is distinguished from mood disorders with psychotic features by the prominence and persistence of psychotic symptoms outside of mood episodes, and from brief or schizophreniform psychoses by its longer duration and functional decline.

narrative.personality: A meticulous, quietly curious retiree, Ervin is used to structuring his days around careful planning, solitary projects, and a strong sense of responsibility toward his family and community.
narrative.stressor: About three years ago, Ervin underwent an unexpected hospitalization for complications related to a minor stroke and subsequent cardiac issues, which abruptly curtailed his ability to do hands-on repairs, yard work, and drive himself to the senior center. The loss of physical independence and the need to rely on others for transportation and medical decisions clashed with his lifelong self-reliant, detail-oriented identity, leaving him increasingly preoccupied with his health and fearful of becoming a burden. Over the following months, his family noticed that he gradually abandoned his gardening, genealogy projects, and community organizing, spending long stretches alone at home and becoming more withdrawn and distant from conversations. As this pattern persisted over two years—with marked decline in his initiative, engagement with hobbies, and participation at the senior center—his wife and adult children convinced him to see a psychiatrist when he stopped returning calls and seemed unable or unwilling to manage routine daily tasks he once handled with ease.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I just don’t feel like doing anything anymore, and I’ve slowly lost interest in the things and people I used to care about.”

narrative.personality: Donna is a rugged, hands-on problem solver who takes pride in her self-reliance, loyalty to her community, and tendency to take on more responsibility than she comfortably can handle.
narrative.stressor: Roughly three years ago, Donna’s shop underwent a major restructuring after being acquired by a larger company, leading to longer shifts, tighter productivity quotas, and pressure to oversee more complex electronic diagnostics with fewer staff. As a lead mechanic and informal mentor to younger workers, she responded by working excessive hours, taking on safety responsibilities, and continuing her volunteer mentoring with 4-H, leaving little time for rest or her usual restorative activities like hiking and music festivals. Over the next year, her coworkers and spouse noticed that she became less talkative in the break room, stopped organizing weekend fishing trips, and began leaving unfinished projects both at work and at home, often sitting quietly in the garage surrounded by unused tools and parts. When this withdrawal and loss of drive persisted despite attempts to cut back her hours—culminating in missed shifts, neglected household tasks, and a stark decline in her engagement with friends and hobbies over more than two years—her husband and shop supervisor encouraged her to seek psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I don’t have the energy or interest to do my work or the things I used to love, and I’ve pulled away from everyone without really knowing why.”

narrative.personality: Marie is an outgoing, talkative caregiver who thrives on lively social interactions, spontaneous community involvement, and bringing warmth and creativity into everyday routines.
narrative.stressor: About three and a half years ago, Marie and her husband went through a prolonged period of marital strain related to financial pressures, disagreements about having another child, and his frequent work-related travel, which left her feeling increasingly unsupported at home. At the same time, conflicts with a demanding parent at the daycare and a tense investigation after an unfounded complaint left her worrying constantly about being blamed or misunderstood, undermining the confidence she once had in her caretaking role. Over the following months, her friends and coworkers noticed a dramatic shift: she stopped organizing potlucks, declined invitations to festivals and concerts, and began sitting quietly during breaks instead of chatting and joking, often staring off and letting classroom preparation tasks slide. As this pattern of emotional blunting, loss of initiative, and social withdrawal deepened and persisted over more than two years—impacting her performance at work, her marriage, and her community involvement—her supervisor, together with her husband, urged her to seek psychiatric help when she began talking about possibly quitting her job because she “just couldn’t bring herself to care anymore.”
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve lost my spark—I don’t feel like talking, going out, or putting effort into anything the way I used to.”
